Tricyrtis affinis is a Japanese woodland species with softly hairy, arching stems and pale lilac-white flowers densely speckled with purple-red spots, held both along the stem and clustered at the tips in late summer and early fall, extending the season of interest in a shaded border well into autumn. Its dependable, showy fall bloom and orchid-like flower detail make it a valuable addition to a shade garden planned for extended seasonal interest, pairing well with fall-blooming anemone, colchicum, and ornamental grasses. Give it consistent moisture and rich soil, and divide clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor and increase the planting.

directions: Plant dormant tubers in fall, 3–4 inches deep, in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Farges' jack-in-the-pulpit is one of the more adaptable and easy-to-grow Chinese Arisaema species, tolerating a wider range of garden conditions than some of its relatives. Arisaema fargesii is a Chinese woodland aroid with broad, three-parted, glossy dark green leaflets often marked with a paler central vein, and a green-and-white striped hooded flower with a distinctive drooping, tongue-like appendage in mid-spring, followed by a spike of red berries in fall. Its relatively easygoing nature and handsome, boldly patterned leaves make it a good entry point into growing Arisaema for gardeners new to the genus, thriving in the same conditions favored by hosta and ferns. As with all Arisaema, the berries and sap contain irritating calcium oxalate crystals, so keep the attractive fall fruit away from pets and children.

Epimedium leptorrhizum is a Chinese species with slender, wide-running rhizomes that let it spread more readily into a groundcover mat than clump-forming epimediums, bearing arrow-shaped, sometimes bronze-mottled leaflets and unusually large, showy, pale pink to lilac flowers with long spurs in mid-spring. Its larger, more colorful flowers and faster spread make it a striking choice for covering a good-sized area of dry shade under trees, where it forms an attractive, weed-suppressing carpet within a few seasons. Cut back old foliage in late winter to fully display the spring flowers, and give it typical epimedium conditions of humus-rich soil with reliable moisture during active growth.

Epimedium stellulatum is a Chinese species forming a semi-evergreen clump of glossy, spiny-margined leaflets, sending up sprays crowded with dozens of small, star-shaped, pure white flowers in early to mid-spring — far more flowers per stem than most epimedium species produce, creating a light, airy, snow-like display above the foliage. Its profuse, dainty white bloom makes an effective contrast planted among darker-leaved hostas or ferns, and the evergreen foliage provides structure through the rest of the year. It spreads at a moderate pace and is easy to grow under standard epimedium conditions, needing division only occasionally to rejuvenate an aging clump.

Epimedium brevicornu is a Chinese species with soft, deciduous, spiny-edged leaflets and delicate sprays of white to pale pink flowers with short, stubby spurs (the source of its common and scientific names) in mid-spring, held on wiry stems above the emerging foliage. Its strong cold hardiness and easy garden adaptability make it one of the more reliable choices for gardeners in colder climates who want to grow epimedium species beyond the typically grown hybrids. It has also long been used in traditional Chinese medicine as a source of yin yang huo, and in the garden it spreads steadily by rhizome to form an attractive, low-maintenance deciduous groundcover.
